title: Beyond-GPU AI Accelerators: Co-Designed Photonic, Analog In-Memory, and Neuromorphic Architectures for Energy-Efficient Neural Computation
background:
The exponential growth of deep neural network workloads has exposed fundamental scaling limits of GPU-based architectures, where data movement across the memory hierarchy now dominates energy consumption and latency. Recent estimates suggest that training frontier models consumes megawatt-scale power, with over 60% of energy spent on DRAM-to-SRAM transfers rather than computation [1]. Three post-CMOS paradigms have emerged to break this 'memory wall': silicon-photonic tensor cores that perform matrix-vector multiplication at the speed of light using Mach-Zehnder interferometer meshes [2], analog in-memory computing (AIMC) using resistive RAM (ReRAM), phase-change memory (PCM), or SRAM crossbars that fuse storage and compute [3], and neuromorphic chips implementing event-driven spiking neural networks (SNNs) for ultra-low-power inference [4]. Demonstrations such as Lightmatter's Envise, IBM's HERMES, and Intel's Loihi 2 have shown 10-100x energy efficiency gains on selected workloads.

Despite these advances, each paradigm faces unresolved technical barriers that prevent broad deployment. Photonic accelerators suffer from thermal drift, limited bit-precision (typically 4-6 bits), and large electro-optic conversion overheads that erode end-to-end gains [2]. AIMC systems struggle with device non-idealities — conductance drift, stochastic write noise, and limited endurance — which degrade model accuracy by 3-15% on ImageNet-scale tasks without compensatory training [3][5]. Neuromorphic platforms lack mature training algorithms; surrogate-gradient SNNs still trail ANN baselines by 2-5 accuracy points on standard benchmarks, and tooling for mapping arbitrary models to event-driven substrates remains immature [4][6]. Cross-cutting gaps include the absence of a unified compiler stack, hardware-aware training methodologies that generalize across substrates, and benchmarking methodology that fairly accounts for analog noise, sparsity, and temporal coding.
challenges: Mitigating analog non-idealities (ReRAM/PCM conductance drift, write stochasticity, IR drop, ADC quantization) while preserving FP32-equivalent accuracy on transformer and large-scale vision workloads
Overcoming photonic precision limits and electro-optic conversion overhead through hybrid optical-electronic dataflows and on-chip thermal calibration that scales to wafer-level interconnect
Closing the accuracy gap between spiking neural networks and ANNs via principled surrogate-gradient training, temporal coding schemes, and ANN-to-SNN conversion that exploits event-driven sparsity

Developing a unified hardware-aware compiler and intermediate representation that maps PyTorch/JAX graphs to heterogeneous photonic, analog, and neuromorphic substrates with automatic precision and noise modeling
Establishing rigorous, reproducible benchmarking that captures end-to-end energy, latency, and accuracy under realistic device variation, beyond peak TOPS/W marketing figures
